guard: The same program on the walker and on the engine produces the same value, the same log, the same refusal, and the same journal entry for entry - the step keys AND their order. (FAIL-FAST suite: markers are upstream of the cells they guard.)

mutations.name: a binary expression evaluates its right operand first, so two effects journal in the wrong order
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: two effects in one binary expression
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: two effects in one binary expression
mutations.note: The value is 2 whichever operand ran first, so nothing about the OUTPUT notices. What notices is the journal: a step key's occurrence is allocated where the effect is reached, so swapping the operands swaps two entries and a resumed run replays into the wrong one.

mutations.name: an argument list is evaluated right to left, so two effects journal in the wrong order
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: two effects in one argument list
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: two effects in one argument list
mutations.note: An argument list has no emitter choice about ORDER - JavaScript evaluates the emitted expression left to right - so the mutation that breaks it is one that reorders the emission. A first attempt reversed the map and reversed it back, which restores every position AND every emitted string: it survived, correctly, because it changed nothing.

mutations.name: a member read is emitted as a native index, so the host prototype is reachable on the engine
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: refusals: a prototype member of a string
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: refusals: a prototype member of a string
mutations.note: A record has NO prototype to reach - `o.constructor` is undefined on both arms - so the cell that catches this is a string's, whose curated table refuses the name L4020. A native index answers the host String constructor there, which is a live capability inside a program that is supposed to have none.

mutations.name: a catch binds the raw thrown value, so a program reads a different error record
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: catching what a refusal throws
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: catching what a refusal throws
mutations.note: `__ctx.caught` rethrows the six classes no program may catch and otherwise hands the walker's frozen {code, kind, message}. `e.code` reads the same either way, which is why this survived until a program logged the WHOLE value: raw, the engine hands back {code, name} - a different record, and one carrying a host class name.

mutations.name: a spread iterates natively, so a record stops being refused
mutations.find: return el.type === "SpreadElement" ? `...${this.seam("iter", this.expr(el.argument as AnyNode))}` : this.expr(el);
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: refusals: not iterable
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: refusals: not iterable
mutations.note: L4015 says arrays and strings and nothing else. A native spread of a record throws a host TypeError instead, which is a different class the program cannot catch the same way.

mutations.name: an object literal's properties are emitted in reverse, so two effects journal backwards
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: two effects in one object literal
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: two effects in one object literal
mutations.note: A record's own key order is observable through `keys`, `entries` and `json.stringify`, and the order its property values were EVALUATED in is observable only in the journal. This moves both.

mutations.name: a template's interpolations are emitted in reverse, so two effects journal backwards
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: two effects in one template
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: two effects in one template
mutations.note: Interpolation is the seam's law, but WHICH value goes into which hole, and in what order the holes were evaluated, is the transform's.

mutations.name: an array literal's elements are emitted in reverse
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: two effects in one array literal
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: two effects in one array literal
mutations.note: The third of the three literal positions where two effects can sit side by side.

mutations.name: a corpus program refuses before it reaches its subject, and the gate calls it identical
mutations.find: ["curated methods", 'const xs = [3, 1, 2]; log(xs.map((x) => x + 1), sort(xs), "AB".toLowerCase(), "a,b".split(","), (2.6).toFixed(1), json.stringify({ a: 1 }));', {}],
mutations.replace: ["curated methods", 'const xs = [3, 1, 2]; log(xs.map((x) => x + 1), sort(xs), "AB".lower(), (2.6).round(), json.stringify({ a: 1 }));', {}],
mutations.expectRed: every corpus program completes, or refuses the code it declares
mutations.cell: every corpus program completes, or refuses the code it declares
mutations.note: The defect this cell was written for, restored: `lower` and `round` are free builtins and not method names, so the program refuses L4014 on BOTH arms before its first log. `identical on both engines` stays green - two arms agreeing on a refusal neither program was written to produce - which is exactly how the string and number tables came to have no passing cell. This is a fixture-discipline cell, so its mutant is in the fixture.

mutations.name: a scope body evaluated at the call, so its effects journal outside the scope
mutations.find: const defers = spec !== undefined && spec.opensScope && spec.optionsAt === 2;
mutations.expectRed: identical on both engines: a fan-out whose body is awaited
mutations.cell: identical on both engines: a fan-out whose body is awaited
mutations.note: The behavioural half of the same rule: both arms journal `fanOut:f` BEFORE the `sleep` inside the body, because the body is evaluated inside the scope. Evaluated at the call, the engine journals the sleep first - a journal the walker's run never wrote, which a resume would then replay against.
